title: HarborBank POC scoping - workload modeling
summary: POC scoping focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling for customer-facing conversational finance assistant. Discussed QPS/concurrency targets, token distributions, latency SLOs, and benchmark plan. Agreed on 6-week pilot with two major benchmark gates and an SE-led throughput test in Redwood Dedicated if needed.
next_steps: Redwood to run initial baseline benchmark with sample traffic (script + sample prompts) - Maya to share test key
HarborBank to provide 48h representative traffic trace + 1000 anonymized prompt examples - Marcus
Schedule SE deep-dive on model variants and quantization (Carlos + Marcus) week of 2026-07-06
Exchange security docs (SOC2 + network diagram) - Maya to share link to security packet
Agree on POC acceptance criteria and finalize scope doc by 2026-07-02
action_items: Maya Chen - Share POC template, pricing framework, and benchmark harness link - 2026-06-28
Marcus Hale - Provide 48h traffic CSV + network topology diagram - 2026-06-30

Samir Patel - Confirm encryption/KMS requirements and data residency constraints - 2026-07-01
transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-06-25 | Time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE); Lena Ortiz (HarborBank Head of AI); Marcus Hale (Infra Lead); Priya Singh (Product PM); Samir Patel (Security)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Carlos is our SE.
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Hi all, thanks. We want to scope a POC to validate cost and latency for our customer chat assistant, and make sure it can handle peak billing queries.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great, goal today is workload characterization, figure QPS, concurrency, token distributions, and agree benchmarks and timeline.
[00:30] Marcus Hale: To start, our current system routes chat through an LLM service in the cloud, average steady-state ~3 QPS for interactive flows, but we see bursts up to 20 QPS around payroll windows and month-end. Concurrency on single-user sessions usually 2-4, but load-testing shows up to 50 concurrent requests hitting the backend during peak retries.
[01:05] Carlos Ruiz: Okay, helpful. When you say 3 QPS steady, is that per region or global?
[01:12] Marcus Hale: That's global for the EU/NA combined; APAC is small so far. Peak 20 is global. The tail is spiky — short bursts 10-30s.
[01:26] Priya Singh: For the assistant, average prompt length is short — about 80 to 150 input tokens, outputs are slightly longer, 120 to 300 tokens depending on the task (explanations, policy text). We also have retrieval-augmented flows where the prompt becomes 400-800 tokens occasionally.
[01:49] Maya Chen: Good detail. So we should model two distributions: typical interactive (input median ~110, output median ~160) and RAG/heavy (input 500, output 300). Any async batch jobs?
[01:59] Marcus Hale: Yes nightly reconciliations that will generate larger batch requests — those are non-latency-sensitive and can be queued, but they can load GPUs if run simultaneous. They could be 200 concurrent small jobs, but spread over a 30‑minute window.
[02:15] Carlos Ruiz: That drives different configuration: for the interactive flow we aim for low p95 latency, so Dedicated with small model variants or Hosted with autoscaling? We'll discuss trade-offs.
[02:25] Lena Ortiz: Our success criteria are twofold: business metric — 90% of queries resolved without human escalation; and infra — p95 latency < 350ms for interactive queries, cost per 1k tokens below our current baseline by at least 10% or at parity with better latency.
[02:44] Maya Chen: Noted. For p95 < 350ms, we need to pin down token rates and model choice. Carlos, thoughts on model selection and quantization?
[02:50] Carlos Ruiz: For that latency goal at 110 input/160 output we typically recommend a 13B quantized variant for Hosted to hit around 180-300ms p95 depending on GPU type and batching. If you need strict SLA we can do Dedicated with pinned capacity and NVLink-enabled GPUs, that'll give more predictable tail latencies. Quantization to int8 or nf4 reduces memory and speeds up KV cache ops but may change output quality slightly — we should run a quality regression on your prompt set.
[03:25] Priya Singh: What's the delta usually in quality when quantizing? We can't accept regressions on financial correctness.
[03:31] Carlos Ruiz: Usually very small for completion/regeneration tasks; but for strict numeric extraction or policy wording, we recommend the eval harness — run 200 representative cases, compute BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics and human review. We'll flag any drift.
[03:45] Marcus Hale: Also important: we need audit logs and KMS integration. Our security team requires customer-managed keys and VPC peering for Private deployment. That will affect timeline.
[03:57] Maya Chen: Understood. For Private, there's an onboarding window. We normally do a lightweight Hosted POC in 2-4 weeks and ramp to Private/Dedicated if acceptance criteria are met. Is that acceptable?
[04:10] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we prefer a staged approach. Start Hosted to validate throughput and cost, then move to Dedicated or Private for production.
[04:20] Carlos Ruiz: On traffic modeling — we recommend Redwood's benchmark harness: synthetic replay from your 48h trace plus synthetic amplification for peaks. We'll measure QPS, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, and cost per 1k tokens. For the POC gate we propose two benchmarks: baseline (week 1) and stress (week 3).
[04:44] Maya Chen: Can you confirm acceptable QPS targets for the baseline?
[04:47] Priya Singh: For baseline, replicate steady-state 3 QPS and run a 10 minute window at 15 QPS to simulate small burst. For stress, simulate sustained 12 QPS for 30 minutes plus a 2-minute spike to 25 QPS.
[05:02] Carlos Ruiz: That maps cleanly. We'll capture concurrency percentiles as well. Also need to know what percent of requests are RAG-heavy — Priya?
[05:10] Priya Singh: Approximately 8% of queries are RAG-heavy currently, but during batch runs it can spike to 20% for reconciliation workflows.
[05:20] Maya Chen: For token distribution, can you provide sample histograms? Marcus said you'll provide traces.
[05:26] Marcus Hale: Yes, we'll export a CSV with timestamp, input_token_count, output_token_count, and request_type flag. An anonymized sample is fine.
[05:34] Maya Chen: Awesome. On benchmarks, we'll run: 1) baseline throughput on Hosted with recommended model; 2) eval quality regression on your 200 prompts; 3) stress test; 4) optional Dedicated run if Hosted fails to meet p95 or cost targets.
[05:51] Carlos Ruiz: For pricing and cost modeling we'll compute token units and weight by model variant. We'll include recommendations: batching size, prefix caching for repeated context, and reranking offload strategies to reduce token churn.
[06:05] Lena Ortiz: Could you explain prefix caching? We've heard the term but not sure how it fits our conversation flows.
[06:10] Carlos Ruiz: Sure — prefix/KV cache stores past key/value states for repeated conversational context so subsequent tokens don't recompute entire attention for history; effectively reduces per-request compute when users have long sessions. Works especially well if your flows reuse similar prompts.
[06:25] Marcus Hale: That sounds helpful. We have 65% of sessions with repeated patterns (account balance, transaction history) so cache hit-rate could be high.
[06:33] Priya Singh: Timeline — we want POC start next week if possible. Can Redwood begin benchmarks with a synthetic trace while we produce the sanitized logs?
[06:41] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll start with our synthetic templates and public sample data, run a quick baseline, and then swap in your trace once available.
[06:49] Samir Patel: Quick security note: our compliance team will need SOC2 report, network topology, and an agent for audit logs to be retained for 12 months. Is that standard?
[06:59] Maya Chen: We have a security packet with SOC2, ISO references, KMS integration notes, and sample network diagrams. We'll share the link after the call. Private deployment supports customer KMS and on-prem routing, but that adds lead time — usually 4–6 weeks for private onboarding.
[07:20] Lena Ortiz: For acceptance criteria, let's write them down: 1) Business: 90% automated resolution on key intents; 2) Infra: p95 < 350ms for interactive traffic; 3) Cost: <= our baseline cost per 1k tokens or improved by 10%; 4) Security: KMS and audit requirements validated.
[07:42] Maya Chen: Agreed. We'll put those into the POC scope doc and assign pass/fail gates.
[07:49] Carlos Ruiz: A few implementation notes: we recommend a warmed KV cache for the stress tests to mimic production sessions, set CPU/GPU affinity for Dedicated trials, and run mixed workloads (interactive + RAG + nightly batch) during stress window.
[08:05] Priya Singh: Can Redwood provide a short script to replay traffic and also a client to run concurrency patterns?
[08:10] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, we'll provide the harness with knobs for QPS, concurrency, token distribution, and spike profiles.
[08:17] Marcus Hale: One more: network egress costs — if Hosted routes cross regions, cost increases. We may prefer regional Dedicated for NA and EU separately.
[08:28] Maya Chen: Good point. We'll include regional routing recommendations and a cost delta estimate.
[08:34] Lena Ortiz: OK, next steps recap?
[08:36] Maya Chen: Redwood: share POC template, benchmark harness, security packet. HarborBank: send anonymized 48h trace, sample prompts, confirm success criteria. SE deep-dive scheduled week of 2026-07-06.
[08:51] Priya Singh: Sounds good, thanks.
[08:54] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the POC doc.
[09:00] End of call.
